draft.title: Solving simultaneous equations with graphs
card: Simultaneous equations are two equations that must both be true at once. Each linear equation draws a straight line.
A point on a line makes that equation true. The point where the two lines cross is on both lines, so it is the solution.
Write the solution as a value of \(x\) and a value of \(y\). Here \(x = 2\) and \(y = 3\). Check it by putting both values into each equation.
Parallel lines have the same gradient and never cross. Two equations whose lines are parallel and different have no solution.

2.alt: The lines \(y = x + 1\) and \(y = -x + 5\) cross at the point \((2, 3)\), shown with dashed guides to \(x = 2\) and \(y = 3\).

draft.remember: The solution is where the lines cross. Parallel lines never cross, so there is none.

a.q: The lines for two equations cross at \((4, -1)\). What is the solution?
a.why: The crossing point is on both lines, so its coordinates solve both equations. The \(x\) value comes first in \((4, -1)\), so swapping them is a mistake.
a.clue: The crossing point is written as \((x, y)\).

b.q: Sam graphs \(y = 2x + 3\) and \(y = 2x - 5\). What does this show about the simultaneous equations?
opts: There is no solution, because the lines are parallel
There is one solution, where the lines meet the \(y\)-axis
There are many solutions, because the gradients match
b.why: Both lines have gradient 2 but different \(y\)-intercepts, so they are parallel and never cross. Matching gradients do not give a solution: they mean the lines never meet.

proposal.title: Solving simultaneous equations with graphs
card: Simultaneous equations are two equations that must both be true at once. Each linear equation draws a straight line.
A point on a line makes that equation true. The point where the two lines cross is on both lines, so it is the solution.

b.q: Lena graphs two linear equations. Her two lines are parallel and different, so they never cross. Which statement is true?
opts: No pair of \(x\) and \(y\) values makes both true
The solutions are where each line meets the \(y\)-axis
Every point on either line is a solution
The solution is the point halfway between the lines
b.why: No point lies on both lines, so no pair of values makes both equations true, and there is no solution. A point on just one line, such as its \(y\)-intercept, makes only that line's equation true.
b.clue: Is any point on both lines?
